source.title: The Anisotropic Noise in Stochastic Gradient Descent: Its Behavior of Escaping from Minima and Regularization Effects
source.authors: Zhan-Xing Zhu; Jing-Feng Wu; Ting Yu; Lei Wu; Jin-Wen Ma

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present, including supplementary material.
record.tranche_reason: The study's experiments compare SGD with full-gradient methods using isotropic and anisotropic noise, reporting generalization results that refine the explanation of SGD's performance. The tested versions do not specifically cover this noise-structure comparison.
record.gate_note: The authors report test-accuracy comparisons among optimization dynamics. Sharpness curves and theoretical indicators are also discussed, but they do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness criterion against training–test gaps. Corrupted-label training does not compare separate natural-label and random-label test performance as required for V1.
record.test_reason: The study tests how gradient-noise structure affects escape from minima and test accuracy, but none of V1–V8 directly. Its sharpness measure uses fixed isotropic perturbations rather than magnitude-aware perturbations; its GD–SGD comparisons do not hold epoch budgets fixed to test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors derive a local escape-efficiency indicator based on noise–curvature alignment, establish conditions favoring aligned anisotropic noise, and provide theoretical and experimental evidence for SGD satisfying those conditions. They argue this helps explain SGD's escape toward flatter, better-generalizing solutions and why isotropic diffusion is insufficient to explain its performance.
record.recipe_differences: Compares SGD with full gradient descent plus isotropic or structured diffusion; does not use the original claim's random-label memorization comparison or the other versions' interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and noise structure change test accuracy; the authors also state that very small learning rates or overly large batches reduce the effect of SGD noise.

fits_no_version.finding: On partially corrupted FashionMNIST, SGD reaches 68.79% test accuracy versus 66.22–66.41% for GD and the recorded isotropic or diagonal-noise dynamics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested diffusion experiment, SGD improves test accuracy more than GD or the tested isotropic and diagonal-noise alternatives.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD outperforms the recorded GD and GLD alternatives on SVHN and CIFAR-10. The extraction mixes Figure 1 and Figure 6 experiments for CIFAR-10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Matching noise magnitude alone does not reproduce SGD's test accuracy in these VGG11 experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that curvature-aligned noise escapes the initial sharp solution and reaches solutions with lower expected isotropic-perturbation sharpness and better test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Curvature alignment of training noise affects escape from sharp minima and subsequent generalization in the tested settings.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 97, 2019
record.problems: The real-dataset comparisons use one stated learning rate per setup; the FashionMNIST experiment uses only 1,200 training examples with 200 randomly mislabeled. Results are presented in figures without uncertainty estimates. The paper does not directly measure the versions' defining behaviors.
record.rows_left_out: No required results omitted; the additional expected-sharpness curves and training-accuracy plots do not directly measure a listed version.

untested.parts: No matched natural-label versus fully random-label training comparison with separate held-out performance. Fitting a partially corrupted training set does not establish this version.
The hidden-width experiment measures noise–curvature alignment, not test error beyond the width required for interpolation.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected generalization comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive-versus-SGD held-out comparison. Adam is used only to train the synthetic networks for the alignment experiment.

No batch-size sweep under a fixed epoch budget or test of recipe adaptations. Full-gradient and minibatch dynamics are compared over iterations; batch-size qualifications in the discussion refer to prior work.
No dropout intervention. Omitting regularization from VGG11 does not test the effect of removing it.

No magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, systematic generalization-gap ranking, or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures. Expected loss increases under fixed isotropic Gaussian perturbations measure a different sharpness construct.
No influence-based identification and removal of memorized examples followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because their measures do not instantiate a listed version. This does not imply that their test-accuracy values are unreadable. Additional noise-aligned methods and Figure 6 experiments are relevant to the study's own question, but are not missing results for a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of fitting fixed random labels versus natural labels with separate held-out performance.
No width sweep testing test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
The study measures expected sharpness under isotropic perturbations, not magnitude-aware sharpness, and does not compare the stated gap-ranking measure.
